title: "Overload, Resource Isolation, and Cascading Failure"
description: "A worked shop microservices lesson."

**Course source:** Day 2 §4 and §5.1. **Running system:** Product, Order and User services.

## One slow dependency can consume an entire service

Suppose Product normally replies in 30 ms, but a database incident raises latency to 5 seconds. Order may accept new requests faster than those waiting on Product complete. In-flight work grows, memory and connection pools fill, and even unrelated Order endpoints become slow. The course calls this **cascading failure** or a service avalanche.

A quick estimate clarifies the mechanism. By Little's law, average in-flight work is approximately

$$
L = \lambda W
$$

where $\lambda$ is throughput in requests per second and $W$ is average time in seconds. At 100 requests/s and 0.03 s, around 3 requests are in flight; at 5 s, around **500** can be in flight if arrival rate is sustained.

## Four complementary protections

**Timeout:** cap waiting for Product. **Bulkhead:** reserve limited concurrency so Product cannot consume every Order resource. **Circuit breaker:** temporarily stop attempting a downstream dependency after repeated failures. **Fallback:** provide a deliberately degraded response when appropriate.

~~~text
Request -> admission limit -> deadline -> Product
                                | failure
                                v
                         circuit / fallback
~~~

These techniques solve different problems. A circuit breaker alone may not limit all resource use; a timeout alone may still permit too many simultaneous requests.

## Tiny conceptual bulkhead

~~~js
let inFlight = 0;
async function guarded(call) {
  if (inFlight >= 20) throw new Error('Busy');
  inFlight++;
  try { return await call(); }
  finally { inFlight--; }
}
~~~

This local counter illustrates the shape of a **single-process** concurrency limit, not a distributed quota. Choose capacity based on downstream concurrency and service-level latency targets.

## Practice

The shop lab simulates an 800 ms Product response with a 350 ms Order timeout. Trigger it with the slow order request and inspect the returned 503. Then imagine 1,000 concurrent callers: a bounded bulkhead would reject excess work rather than allowing unlimited waiting.

## Review questions

What failure does this technique address? Which state belongs to the caller and which belongs to the provider? What would you measure to confirm that it works?
